title: Intergenerational transmission of depression and anxiety among diverse immigrant populations in Sweden
content:
by Kenta Okuyama, Sara Larsson Lönn, Tsuyoshi Hamano, Ardavan M. Khoshnood, Jan Sundquist, Kristina Sundquist

Background

Little is known about the intergenerational transmission of depression and anxiety among children to immigrants. Our study aimed to investigate the association between parental depression/anxiety and offspring depression/anxiety among non-immigrants and second-generation immigrants, and whether the association differs by sex and immigrants’ regions of origin.

Methods

We used nationwide longitudinal registers that cover the entire population in Sweden. The study individuals were categorized as non-immigrants (n = 744,089) and second-generation immigrants (n = 210,868) from six regions of origin. Parental and offspring depression and anxiety were assessed by registered diagnosis from the National Patient Register, and the association was examined by Cox proportional hazard models, adjusted for potential confounders.

Findings

Parental depression and anxiety were associated with increased risks of depression and anxiety among offspring of non-immigrants and second-generation immigrants and the strength of the associations differed by sex and immigrants’ region of origin. Overall, the associations were weaker among second-generation immigrants than non-immigrants. No association was found among second-generation immigrant females from Latin America. The association with maternal depression and anxiety was more pronounced (compared with paternal) among second-generation immigrant males and females from Africa.

Conclusions

The findings indicate potentially different mechanisms by region of origin and sex in the intergenerational transmission of depression and anxiety. Underlying factors of the weaker association of parental and offspring depression and anxiety among second-generation immigrants could be investigated in future studies.
